results.title: The fixed-effects model for robust analysis of stepped-wedge cluster trials with a small number of clusters and continuous outcomes: a simulation study
results.content: We recommend the fixed-effects model for robust analysis of SW-CTs with a small number of clusters and continuous outcomes, due to its proper type I error control and ability to automatically adjust for all potential imbalanced time-invariant cluster-level covariates and confounders. In this article, we present a simulation study to compare the performance of the fixed-effects model against the mixed-effects model in the analyses of cross-sectional SW-CTs with small numbers of clusters, continuous outcomes, cluster-level covariate imbalances, and cluster-level confounding. In doing so, we aim to address notable gaps in the SW-CT literature (i.) concerning the performance of the fixed-effects model in controlling for inflated type I error rates in trials with continuous outcomes and (ii.) by explicitly demonstrating the fixed-effects model’s ability to automatically adjust for all time-invariant cluster-level covariate imbalance and confounding. Comparison of the fixed-effects model (FE), mixed-effects model (ME), and covariate-adjusted mixed-effects model (ME adj) in terms of relative bias (%), precision, coverage probability, type I error, power, and root mean square error in scenarios with no cluster-level covariate imbalance or confounding. However, like the previous scenarios with no cluster-level covariate imbalance or confounding, the mixed-effects model with and without adjustment often had low coverage probabilities and inflated type I errors especially with a small number of clusters or when the ICC was low (Fig.5). In this article, we fill gaps in the SW-CT literature concerning the performance of the fixed-effects model in maintaining correct type I error and automatically adjusting for all cluster-level covariate imbalance and confounding. In this article, we present a simulation study to compare the performance of the fixed-effects model against the mixed-effects model in the analyses of cross-sectional SW-CTs with small numbers of clusters, continuous outcomes, cluster-level covariate imbalances, and cluster-level confounding. In doing so, we aim to address notable gaps in the SW-CT literature (i.) concerning the performance of the fixed-effects model in controlling for inflated type I error rates in trials with continuous outcomes and (ii.) by explicitly demonstrating the fixed-effects model’s ability to automatically adjust for all time-invariant cluster-level covariate imbalance and confounding. In scenarios with (i.) no cluster-level covariate imbalance or confounding, we observe that the fixed-effects and unadjusted and covariate-adjusted mixed-effects models were relatively unbiased (Fig. 2). However, like the previous scenarios with no cluster-level covariate imbalance or confounding, the mixed-effects model with and without adjustment often had low coverage probabilities and inflated type I errors especially with a small number of clusters or when the ICC was low (Fig. 5). In this article, we only simulated cluster-level covariate imbalance to focus on how specifying cluster intercepts as fixed in a fixed-effects model can automatically adjust for these imbalances in a SW-CT. results.title: Sample size considerations for stratified cluster randomization design with binary outcomes and varying cluster size
results.content: We propose closed-form sample size formulas for estimating the required total number of subjects and for estimating the number of clusters for each group per stratum, based on Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel statistic for stratified cluster randomization design with binary outcomes, accounting for both clustering and varying cluster size. In this paper, we propose closed-form sample size formulas for estimating the required total number of subjects and for estimating the number of clusters for each group per stratum, for stratified CRTs with binary outcomes and varying cluster size. In Section 2, we present notations and the method for sample size estimations for the required total number of subjects and for the number of clusters for each group per stratum based on Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel statistic, adjusting for both clustering and varying cluster size. Then, the sample size can be obtained by solving the following two equations: Based on Equations (1) and (2), the total number of subjects _N_ required for stratified cluster randomization design is given by The estimated total number of subjects _N_ depends on the mean and variance of the distribution of cluster size, in addition to the expected group difference, ICC, and type _I_ and type _II_ error. We conduct simulation studies to assess the performance of the proposed sample size approach for estimating the required number of clusters for each group per stratum for stratified CRTs with varying cluster size, under various design configurations. This suggests that the proposed method derived based on the large sample theory is widely applicable to stratified CRTs with varying cluster size and maintains the desired power in scenarios where the number of clusters per group per stratum is relatively small. This paper presents closed-form sample size formulas for estimating the required total number of subjects and for estimating the number of clusters for each group per stratum, based on Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel statistic, for stratified cluster randomization design with binary outcomes and varying cluster size.

results.title: Design and analysis of cluster randomized trials with time-to-event outcomes under the additive hazards mixed model
results.content: First, we discuss improved inference for the treatment effect parameter via bias-corrected sandwich variance estimators and randomization-based test under AHMM, addressing potential small-sample biases in CRTs. Next, we derive a new sample size formula for AHMM analysis of CRTs accommodating both equal and unequal cluster sizes. Their sample size formula relies on the ICC defined based on the censoring indicators instead of the failure times, which may not fully capture the dependency structure of the time-to-event outcomes.13 To date, the optimal definition of the ICC for censored survival outcomes is debatable.14 Zhong and Cook13 refined the sample size formula under the marginal Cox proportional hazards model by numerically computing the asymptotic sandwich variance expression of the hazard ratio estimator, based on the assumed bivariate survival functions for the failure times as well as for the censoring times induced by copulas, but under equal cluster sizes. With non-censored continuous or binary outcomes, the sandwich variance estimator of the traditional GEE estimator has been shown to have negative bias and inflate the type I error rate of the Wald _z_- or _t_-test when the number of clusters is small.28 To maintain the nominal level of rejection under the null (and to ensure validity of the test), appropriate analysis of CRTs should account for such finite-sample bias in variance estimation, possibly through a bias-corrected sandwich variance estimator.28–31 Although there are several previous studies reporting simulation comparisons of different bias-corrected sandwich variance estimators for CRT applications,24,26,42,43 their development and findings are currently restricted to non-censored outcomes. Empirical type I error rates for the Wald _t_-test and randomization test from a simulation study based on different parameter configurations of the baseline hazard (_λ_ 0(_t_)), frailty variance (_σ_ 2), average cluster size , and estimated number of clusters when the coefficient of variation of cluster size is 0. Predicted and empirical power for the Wald _t_-test and randomization test from a simulation study based on different parameter configurations of the baseline hazard (_λ_ 0(_t_)), effect size (_δ_), frailty variance (_σ_ 2), average cluster size , and estimated number of clusters when the coefficient of variation of cluster size is 0. Second, while the statistical analysis with all bias-corrected sandwich variance estimators and the randomization test can easily accommodate cluster-level or participant-level covariates, our sample size procedure assumes an unadjusted AHMM without additional covariates.
